docs.title: Hardware and wiring
docs.text:
This page lists the parts you need and shows how to connect the ESP32 to the tub.

Mains voltage

A spa contains mains voltage and can deliver a large fault current. Turn off the spa at its breaker before you open the equipment bay or touch the control board. Check that the board is dead before you work on it. If you are not competent to work near mains wiring, get an electrician to do it. Read Safety first.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Part Why you need it An ESP32 board Runs ESPHome and the spa_bus component. An RS485 transceiver Converts the bus's differential signal to the 3.3 V serial signal of the ESP32. A differential signal is carried as the voltage difference between two wires, A and B. Twisted-pair cable Carries A and B. Twisting the pair rejects electrical noise from pumps and heaters. A DC power supply for the ESP32 Powers the ESP32 independently of the tub. See Power. A connector that fits the tub's RS485 header Lets you unplug the ESP32 without cutting wires.

You can use one of two hardware options.

Waveshare ESP32-S3-ETH-8DI-8ROAny ESP32 and a transceiver module

The project's example device uses this board. It has an ESP32-S3, an onboard RS485 transceiver, Ethernet, 8 relays and 8 digital inputs. The RS485 transceiver connects to GPIO17 (TX) and GPIO18 (RX).

The example YAML sets no flow_control_pin, because the onboard transceiver switches between send and receive by itself. Check the board's schematic if you use a different revision.

The ready-made device file is esphome/example-jacuzzibridge-esp.yaml.

Any ESP32 with a free UART works. Add a 3.3 V RS485 transceiver module, for example one based on a MAX3485 or SP3485 chip. Do not use a 5 V MAX485 module directly: its receive output can put 5 V on an ESP32 pin, and ESP32 pins tolerate 3.3 V only.

  • Connect the module's RO (receiver output) to the ESP32's RX pin.
  • Connect the module's DI (driver input) to the ESP32's TX pin.
  • Many modules have DE (driver enable) and RE (receiver enable) pins. DE turns on the transmitter. RE turns on the receiver. Tie them together and connect them to a spare GPIO, then set that GPIO as flow_control_pin. The component then turns the transmitter on only while it sends. Some modules switch direction automatically and have no DE/RE pins. Those need no flow_control_pin.

docs.title: The tub's RS485 header
docs.text:
The J235 control board has an RS485 header for a second topside panel. A topside panel is the control panel on the rim of the tub. Most tubs have only one panel, so the second-panel header is usually free. It is the intended place to attach a monitoring device.

The bus is shared. The control board, the topside panel and any add-on device sit on the same two wires. The control board decides who may talk:

  • The board broadcasts a status frame about three times per second. Every device on the bus hears it. This is all the ESP32 needs in receive-only mode.
  • The board polls each panel channel in turn with a clear-to-send frame (CTS). A channel is a bus address that the board has given to one client. A client may transmit only in the short gap right after the CTS for its own channel.
  • A new device must ask the board for a channel before it can send. The ESP32 does this only when transmit is enabled and you issue the first command.

A receive-only ESP32 never drives the bus, so it cannot collide with the topside panel. See the wire protocol for the details.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
ESP32 to spa RS485 wiring The spa control board RS485 header has four connections: plus 12 volts, 0 volts, A and B. Connect A to A, B to B and 0 volts to the transceiver ground. Do not connect plus 12 volts unless you know the header's current rating. The RS485 transceiver connects to the ESP32: transceiver RO to GPIO18 (RX), GPIO17 (TX) to transceiver DI, and an optional flow control GPIO to DE and RE if the transceiver needs it. The ESP32 board takes power from its own DC supply. Spa (mains: isolate first) Control board RS485 header for a second topside panel RS485 transceiver onboard (Waveshare) or MAX3485 / SP3485 module ESP32 UART 115200 8N1 Own DC supply check the board's input range +12 V 0 V A B GND A (+) B (-) RO DI DE / RE GPIO18 (RX) GPIO17 (TX) flow_control_pin A to A B to B common ground twisted pair not connected receive transmit optional Solid line: connect. Dashed line: only when needed. Cross: do not connect unless you know the header's rating. Use a transceiver with 3.3 V logic, the same as the ESP32.
  1. Connect header A to transceiver A (sometimes labelled A+ or D+).
  2. Connect header B to transceiver B (sometimes labelled B- or D-).
  3. Connect header 0 V to the transceiver's ground. RS485 tolerates some ground difference, but a common ground keeps the signal within the transceiver's range and makes reception reliable.
  4. Leave the header's +12 V unconnected unless you have read Power.

A and B swapped

Manufacturers do not agree on which wire is A and which is B. If the ESP32 logs no status frames and the UART settings are correct, swap A and B. A swap does no damage.

Termination

RS485 buses use a 120 ohm resistor at each end to stop signal reflections. The tub's own wiring is short and already works with its panel. Leave the transceiver's termination resistor or jumper off unless reception is unreliable.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The tub's header carries 12 V. The legacy wiring notes for the J235 list it as "12v +/, A/B": a 12 V supply pair and the A/B pair. The current rating of that 12 V supply is not known. The supply also feeds the topside panel. An ESP32 with Wi-Fi can draw short peaks of several hundred milliamps. Overloading the supply could disturb the panel or the board.

Power the ESP32 from its own supply unless you know the header's rating.

  • The Waveshare ESP32-S3-ETH-8DI-8RO takes 7-36 V DC on its power terminal, or 5 V over USB-C. Check your board's documentation for its input range before you connect any supply.
  • Other ESP32 boards usually take 5 V over USB. Check the board's documentation.

If you decide to use the header's 12 V, use a board or a regulator that accepts 12 V, and add a fuse in the 12 V line.

docs.title: UART settings
docs.text:
The bus runs at 115200 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit (115200 8N1). The tub definition sets the baud rate. ESPHome checks at compile time that your uart: block matches it. The uart: defaults for data bits, parity and stop bits are already 8N1.

Set logger: baud_rate: 0 on boards where the logger would share the bus UART. This keeps log output off the RS485 pins. Logs still reach you over Wi-Fi through the API.

docs.title: Mounting
docs.text:
• Mount the ESP32 in a dry enclosure, away from the heater and the pumps. The equipment bay gets hot and humid.
  • Route the low-voltage cable away from mains cables, and fix it so it cannot touch moving or hot parts.
  • Close every cover before you restore power at the breaker.

Next: Build and flash.

docs.title: Build and flash
docs.text:
This page builds the ESPHome firmware for the tub bridge, flashes it, and checks that it receives the tub's status. Wire the hardware first: see Hardware and wiring.

Use a current ESPHome release. The project's CI checks the component against the latest ESPHome release, and these examples were checked with ESPHome 2026.10. You can use the ESPHome Device Builder add-on in Home Assistant, or the esphome command line tool. The steps are the same in both.

The complete example device file is esphome/example-jacuzzibridge-esp.yaml. The steps below explain each part of it.

docs.title: 1. Add the secrets
docs.text:
ESPHome reads !secret values from a file called secrets.yaml in the same folder as your device file. Secrets keep passwords and keys out of the device file, so you can share the device file safely.

secrets.yaml
wifi_ssid: "YourNetwork"
wifi_password: "your-wifi-password"
jacuzzibridge_api_key: "base64-key-from-esphome.io"

jacuzzibridge_api_key encrypts the link between the ESP32 and Home Assistant. Generate a new random key on the ESPHome native API page, or with openssl rand -base64 32. Do not reuse a key from another device.

docs.title: 2. Create the device file
docs.text:
Start with the device basics. friendly_name sets the device name in Home Assistant, and Home Assistant builds each entity ID from it. Keep Jacuzzi J235 if you plan to switch over from the MQTT bridge, because the entity IDs then stay the same.

jacuzzibridge-esp.yaml
esphome:
  name: jacuzzibridge-esp
  friendly_name: Jacuzzi J235

esp32:
  variant: esp32s3          # match your board
  framework:
    type: arduino

wifi:
  ssid: !secret wifi_ssid
  password: !secret wifi_password

logger:
  baud_rate: 0              # keep log output off the UART; logs still reach you over the API

api:
  encryption:
    key: !secret jacuzzibridge_api_key

ota:
  - platform: esphome

docs.title: 3. Add the component, pinned to a release
docs.text:
external_components tells ESPHome where to download spa_bus. Pin it to a release tag such as v2.0.0. Find the latest tag on the releases page.

external_components:
  - source: github://srleach/spa2mqtt@v2.0.0
    components: [spa_bus]

Pinning matters for three reasons:

  • Repeatable builds. A tag always points to the same code. If you build from main instead, a rebuild months later can pick up changes you did not test.
  • Matching definitions. The component reads the tub definition from the same download. The tag fixes the definition too.
  • Controlled updates. You update by changing the tag on purpose, after you read the release notes. See Releases and versions for what a version number change means.

docs.title: Option A: the package with every entity
docs.text:
A package is a YAML file that ESPHome merges into your device file. The J235 package lists every entity in the J235 definition. Use the same tag as the component, because the package names entity keys that this version of the component must know.

packages:
  spa_entities: github://srleach/spa2mqtt/esphome/packages/jacuzzi_j235.yaml@v2.0.0

The package gives each entity an id such as spa_current_temperature. To change one entity, declare it again in your device file with the same id. ESPHome merges your settings over the package's settings.

docs.title: Option B: choose entities one at a time
docs.text:
Leave out packages: and declare only the entities you want. Each one uses platform: spa_bus and an entity: key from the tub definition. ESPHome stops the build if the key does not exist, or if it belongs to a different platform.

sensor:
  - platform: spa_bus
    entity: current_temperature
    name: Current Water Temperature
    device_class: temperature
    unit_of_measurement: °C
    state_class: measurement
    accuracy_decimals: 1

binary_sensor:
  - platform: spa_bus
    entity: heater_active
    name: Heater Active
    device_class: heat

text_sensor:
  - platform: spa_bus
    entity: pump_1_speed
    name: Pump 1 Speed
Platform J235 entity keys sensor current_temperature, setpoint_temperature, filter_change_days, water_change_days, uv_days, display_state, secondary_value_raw binary_sensor circulation_pump_status, secondary_pump_status, main_pump_status, manual_circulation_call, heater_active, set_mode_active text_sensor pump_1_speed button temperature_increment, temperature_decrement, pump_1_button, pump_2_button, light_button number temperature_set_control

The Pump 1, Pump 1 Low, Pump 2 and Light switches and Light Mode of the MQTT bridge are not available here: the component has no switch platform yet, and it does not decode the lights frame. Use the pump and light buttons.

Keep the name values from the package if you want the same entity IDs as the MQTT bridge.

docs.title: 5. Add the UART and the hub
docs.text:
The uart: block configures the ESP32 serial port that connects to the RS485 transceiver. The spa_bus: block is the hub. The hub reads the UART, decodes the frames and feeds every spa_bus entity.

uart:
  - id: spa_uart
    tx_pin: GPIO17          # to the transceiver's DI
    rx_pin: GPIO18          # from the transceiver's RO
    baud_rate: 115200
    rx_buffer_size: 512

spa_bus:
  id: spa
  uart_id: spa_uart
  definition: jacuzzi_j235  # a definition name, or a path to your own definition YAML
  transmit: false           # receive-only; see "Enable transmit" below
  heartbeat: 60s            # republish every entity this often, even without a change
  # flow_control_pin: GPIO21   # only if your transceiver has DE/RE wired to a GPIO
  bus_state:
    name: Bus State
Key Default Meaning definition required Tub definition name or alias from definitions/, or a path to a .yaml file relative to the device file. transmit false Allow the component to send to the tub. flow_control_pin none GPIO that drives the transceiver's DE/RE pins while sending. heartbeat 60s Interval for republishing every value. bus_state none Diagnostic text sensor with the link state. Takes the usual text sensor options.

The larger rx_buffer_size gives the ESP32 room to hold a burst of bus traffic while Wi-Fi is busy.

docs.title: 6. First flash over USB
docs.text:
The first flash must use a USB cable, because the chip does not yet run ESPHome and cannot accept an update over the network.

Command lineESPHome Device Builder 
esphome run jacuzzibridge-esp.yaml

Choose the USB serial port when ESPHome asks.

Open the device, select Install, then Plug into the computer running ESPHome Device Builder or Plug into this computer.

Some ESP32-S3 boards need the BOOT button held while you plug in the cable, to enter the download mode.

After the first flash, ESPHome updates the device over Wi-Fi (OTA, over-the-air). You do not need the cable again unless the firmware fails to start. You can do the first flash on the bench before you install the ESP32 in the tub.

docs.title: 7. Check the logs
docs.text:
Watch the logs with esphome logs jacuzzibridge-esp.yaml, or select Logs in the Device Builder. With the ESP32 wired to the tub, you should see:

[C][spa_bus]: Spa bus:
[C][spa_bus]:   Transmit: disabled (receive-only)
[C][spa_bus]:   Fields: ...
[I][spa_bus]: receiving status frames
  • receiving status frames means that the ESP32 decodes valid status frames from the control board. The entities now have values.
  • The Bus State sensor shows receive-only. That is the normal state while transmit: false.
  • Bus State shows no status and the log shows no status frames for 10000 ms if no valid status frame arrives for 10 s. Check the wiring, swap A and B, and check the baud rate.
  • The configuration dump also prints frame and CRC error counts. CRC (cyclic redundancy check) errors mean that frames arrive damaged. A few at start-up are normal. A steady rise points to a wiring or ground problem.

Then add the device in Home Assistant. Home Assistant usually discovers it and shows a notification. Select Configure and enter the API key from secrets.yaml.

docs.title: Before the repository is public
docs.text:
Private repository

While srleach/spa2mqtt is private, the github:// shorthand cannot download it. Use the long git form with a GitHub token. Create a fine-grained personal access token with read-only Contents access to this one repository. Store it in secrets.yaml as github_token.

external_components:
  - source:
      type: git
      url: https://github.com/srleach/spa2mqtt
      ref: v2.0.0
      username: your-github-user
      password: !secret github_token
    components: [spa_bus]

packages:
  spa_entities:
    url: https://github.com/srleach/spa2mqtt
    ref: v2.0.0
    username: your-github-user
    password: !secret github_token
    files: [esphome/packages/jacuzzi_j235.yaml]

ESPHome also accepts the token inside the URL, as https://<token>@github.com/srleach/spa2mqtt. The username and password form is better, because the token stays in secrets.yaml and out of the device file. Switch back to the github:// shorthand when the repository is public, and revoke the token.

docs.title: Enable transmit
docs.text:
Untested on a real tub

The transmit path is tested against a simulated control board only. Enable it only if you accept that risk, and stay near the tub the first time.

With transmit: false, the buttons and the Temperature Set Control number appear in Home Assistant but do nothing. The log shows transmit disabled (spa_bus.transmit: false); ignoring press 0x01.

To enable transmit:

  1. Set transmit: true in the spa_bus: block.
  2. If your transceiver has DE/RE wired to a GPIO, set flow_control_pin.
  3. Install the new firmware over the air.

Enabling transmit sends nothing by itself. The ESP32 stays silent until you press a button or change the setpoint. On the first command:

  1. The Bus State sensor changes from listening to claiming. The ESP32 looks for a free channel on the bus.
  2. The J235 has no free channel, so the ESP32 sends a channel request when the board next offers one. Bus State shows requested.
  3. The board answers with a channel number. Bus State shows ready, followed by the channel, for example ready (0x11).
  4. The ESP32 sends the queued button press in its channel's time slot. The topside reacts as if you had pressed its button.

The setpoint number presses Temp up or Temp down until the tub's setpoint matches the target. The first press on the J235 only opens the set screen, so the component waits for the set screen to appear before it steps. See the wire protocol for how this was worked out.

To go back to receive-only, set transmit: false and install the firmware again.

docs.title: Switch over from MQTT
docs.text: This page moves an existing install from the MQTT bridge to the ESPHome component. If you follow the steps in order, Home Assistant keeps the same entity IDs. Your dashboards, automations and long-term statistics keep working.

docs.title: How the entity IDs survive
docs.text:
Home Assistant stores each entity in its entity registry under two names:

  • The unique ID is the integration's own key for the entity. Home Assistant uses it to recognise the entity after a restart.
  • The entity ID, such as sensor.jacuzzi_j235_current_water_temperature, is the name that dashboards, automations and history use.

Long-term statistics are stored against the entity ID. They follow the entity ID, so they survive the switch if the new entity gets the old entity ID.

The ESPHome device is a new device in a different integration, so its entities get new unique IDs. Home Assistant builds each new entity ID from the device's friendly_name and the entity's name. With friendly_name: Jacuzzi J235 and the names from the package, ESPHome asks for exactly the IDs the MQTT bridge used.

Home Assistant gives an entity ID to only one entity at a time. While the MQTT entities still exist, the ESPHome entities get a suffix such as _2. That is why you delete the MQTT device before you adopt the ESP32.

Before After Device Jacuzzi J235, MQTT integration Jacuzzi J235, ESPHome integration Entity IDs sensor.jacuzzi_j235_current_water_temperature, ... the same History and long-term statistics stored under the entity ID the same records continue Unique IDs bare definition keys, for example current_temperature ESPHome's own unique IDs Device ID, area, device-based automations MQTT device new device: set the area again, and update automations that use device triggers or device actions Commands need spa.transmit: true on the bridge need transmit: true on the ESP32

Device-based automations

Automations built with the visual editor's Device triggers and actions refer to the device ID, which changes. Automations that use entity triggers and actions keep working. Look for device-based automations before you start, so you know what to fix afterwards.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
1. Build and test the ESP32 firmware on the bench. Follow Build and flash, but do not add the device to Home Assistant yet. This keeps the downtime short.
  2. Make a Home Assistant backup. It is your fallback if a step goes wrong.
  3. Note any entity that you renamed by hand in Home Assistant. A renamed entity ID is stored in the registry, and the ESP32 will not reproduce it. Rename the new entity to match after the switch.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Stop the bridge. Stop the spa2mqtt container, for example with docker compose stop spa2mqtt or Stop on the Portainer stack. Two readers on the bus are harmless, but a running bridge would publish the MQTT device again after you delete it.
  2. Delete the MQTT device. In Home Assistant, go to Settings > Devices & services > MQTT, open the Jacuzzi J235 device, and select Delete. This releases the entity IDs. Home Assistant also clears the bridge's retained discovery messages, so the device does not come back.
  3. Install the ESP32. Isolate the spa at its breaker, wire the ESP32 to the RS485 header as shown in Hardware and wiring, close the covers and restore power.
  4. Adopt the ESP32. In Settings > Devices & services, Home Assistant shows the discovered ESPHome device. Select Configure and enter the API key.
  5. Check the entity IDs. Open the new device. Each entity ID should match the old one, for example sensor.jacuzzi_j235_current_water_temperature. If an entity ID has a _2 suffix, the old entity was not deleted. Delete the old entity under Settings > Entities, then rename the new one to remove the suffix.
  6. Check the history. Open the water temperature entity. The history graph should show the old MQTT values followed by the new ESPHome values.

If you used the MQTT entities only on a dashboard, nothing else needs to change.

docs.title: Roll back
docs.text:
You can go back to the MQTT bridge at any time.

  1. In Home Assistant, delete the Jacuzzi J235 ESPHome device under Settings > Devices & services > ESPHome. This releases the entity IDs again.
  2. Power off the ESP32 or disconnect it from the bus. This is not needed for safety while it is receive-only, but it stops the device from appearing again.
  3. Start the bridge container again. It republishes its MQTT discovery messages, and Home Assistant creates the entities with the old unique IDs and entity IDs.

Restore order

The bridge's entities take the old entity IDs only if the ESPHome entities are gone first. Delete the ESPHome device before you start the bridge.

docs.title: Install with Docker Compose
docs.text:
This guide runs the MQTT bridge from the published container image with Docker Compose. Docker Compose is the Docker tool that starts containers from a YAML file. You need a Docker host that can reach your RS485-to-TCP adapter and your MQTT broker.

The image is ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt. It is built for linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and linux/arm/v7, so it runs on a PC, a Raspberry Pi or most NAS devices.

Check the bus first

Run the read-only monitor once before you install. It proves that the adapter and the tub definition work. See Getting started.

docs.title: 1. Get the files
docs.text:
You need two files from the repository's deploy/ folder. Put them in a new folder on the Docker host, for example ~/spa2mqtt.

mkdir -p ~/spa2mqtt && cd ~/spa2mqtt
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srleach/spa2mqtt/main/deploy/docker-compose.yml
curl -fsSL -o .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srleach/spa2mqtt/main/deploy/.env.example
  • docker-compose.yml describes the container. You do not need to edit it.
  • .env holds your settings. Docker Compose reads it for two reasons: to choose the image tag, and to pass the settings into the container as environment variables.

docs.title: 2. Edit the settings
docs.text:
Open .env and set at least these values:

Variable Set it to SPA_IP The address of your RS485-to-TCP adapter SPA_PORT The adapter's TCP port (8899 for an EW11A in its usual setup) MQTT_BROKER The address of the MQTT broker that Home Assistant uses MQTT_USERNAME, MQTT_PASSWORD The broker login, or empty for an open broker

Leave SPA_TRANSMIT=false for now. The bridge then only listens to the tub. See Configuration for every setting.

.env contains your MQTT password. Make it readable only by you:

chmod 600 .env

docs.title: Optional: use a config.yml
docs.text:
Some settings have no environment variable, for example the ha: section (unique_id_prefix, legacy_topics, device_name) and a USB serial adapter. For those, create a config.yml next to docker-compose.yml and uncomment the volumes: lines in docker-compose.yml. The container reads it at /app/config.yml. Values in .env still override the same values in config.yml.

curl -fsSL -o config.yml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/srleach/spa2mqtt/main/config.yml.example

The container runs as an unprivileged user (user ID 10001), so that user must be able to read the file. A file with mode 600 owned by your own account fails to load. Keep the MQTT password in .env and make config.yml world-readable with chmod 644 config.yml.

docs.title: 3. Start it
docs.text:
docker compose up -d

Docker pulls the image and starts the container in the background. The container restarts by itself after a reboot or a crash (restart: unless-stopped).

In Home Assistant, open Settings > Devices & services > MQTT. A device named after the tub definition, for example Jacuzzi J235, appears within a few seconds. Its buttons and the setpoint show as unavailable while transmit is off. That is expected.

docs.title: Read the logs
docs.text:
The logs show the connection to the adapter and the broker, and every warning.

docker compose logs -f spa2mqtt

Press Ctrl-C to stop following. To see more detail, set LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG in .env and run docker compose up -d again.

docs.title: Run the read-only monitor
docs.text:
The monitor decodes the bus to your terminal and never transmits. Stop the bridge first, because most adapters accept only one TCP client.

docker compose stop spa2mqtt
docker compose run --rm spa2mqtt spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.100
docker compose start spa2mqtt

The monitor does not read .env. Add -p PORT and -d DEFINITION if yours are not 8899 and jacuzzi_j235. For a Jacuzzi J345 behind a ProLink module:

docker compose run --rm spa2mqtt spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.50 -p 4257 -d jacuzzi_j345

The J345 guide has the .env values for that tub.

See Monitor and capture for the monitor's options.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
SPA2MQTT_TAG=2 follows the newest 2.x.y release. A new major version (3.0.0) can contain breaking changes, so the tag does not move to it by itself. To upgrade within the pinned tag:

docker compose pull
docker compose up -d

pull downloads the newest image for the tag. up -d recreates the container only if the image changed. To remove old images afterwards, run docker image prune.

Read the release notes before you change the major version.

docs.title: Roll back
docs.text:
Every release has its own image tag. To go back, pin the version you want in .env:

SPA2MQTT_TAG=2.0.0

Then run docker compose up -d. The container stays on that version until you change the line again. See Releases and versions for the tag scheme.

docs.title: Enable transmit
docs.text:
Transmit lets Home Assistant press the tub's buttons and change the setpoint. Enable it only after the decoded values match the topside, and read Safety first.

  1. In .env, set SPA_TRANSMIT=true.
  2. Run docker compose up -d. Compose recreates the container with the new value.
  3. Check the log. It shows TRANSMIT ENABLED: commands from Home Assistant will be sent to the tub.

The bridge still sends nothing at start-up. It claims a bus channel only when the first command arrives from Home Assistant. To go back to receive-only, set SPA_TRANSMIT=false and run docker compose up -d again.

docs.title: Stop and remove
docs.text:
docker compose down

This removes the container. Home Assistant marks the entities unavailable. The device stays in Home Assistant until you delete it there.

docs.title: Install with Portainer
docs.text:
Portainer is a web interface for Docker. In Portainer, a stack is a group of containers defined by a Docker Compose file. This guide gives two ways to deploy spa2mqtt as a stack.

Method Use it when A. Stack from the published image Normal use. Fast, nothing to build. B. Stack from the repository Fallback. The host cannot pull from ghcr.io, or you want to run a branch that has no image.

Both methods take every setting from environment variables and use no bind mounts. A bind mount maps a file from the host into the container. Portainer under Home Assistant OS keeps its stack files in a folder that the host cannot see, and the host's /data is read-only. A bind mount there fails with mkdir /data: read-only file system. Environment variables avoid that problem.

Check the bus first

Run the read-only monitor once before you install. See Run the read-only monitor below.

docs.title: A. Stack from the published image
docs.text:
1. In Portainer, open your environment and select Stacks > Add stack.
  2. Set Name to spa2mqtt.

  3. Select Web editor. Paste the contents of deploy/portainer-stack.yml:

    # spa2mqtt stack for Portainer: published image, settings from environment variables only.
#
# Paste this into Portainer > Stacks > Add stack > Web editor, then add the variables in
# the "Environment variables" section below the editor. SPA_IP and MQTT_BROKER are required.
# There are no volumes on purpose: Portainer on Home Assistant OS cannot bind-mount files
# ("mkdir /data: read-only file system").
#
# Guide: https://seanrleach.co.uk/spa2mqtt/install/portainer/
# Jacuzzi J345 through a ProLink module: SPA_IP = the ProLink's address, SPA_PORT=4257,
# SPA_DEFINITION=jacuzzi_j345. See https://seanrleach.co.uk/spa2mqtt/tubs/jacuzzi-j345/

services:
  spa2mqtt:
    image: ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt:${SPA2MQTT_TAG:-2}
    container_name: spa2mqtt
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SPA_IP: ${SPA_IP:?Set SPA_IP to the RS485-to-TCP adapter address}
      SPA_PORT: ${SPA_PORT:-8899}
      SPA_DEFINITION: ${SPA_DEFINITION:-jacuzzi_j235}
      # SAFETY: false = receive-only. Read the Safety page before you set true.
      SPA_TRANSMIT: ${SPA_TRANSMIT:-false}
      MQTT_BROKER: ${MQTT_BROKER:?Set MQTT_BROKER to the MQTT broker address}
      MQTT_PORT: ${MQTT_PORT:-1883}
      MQTT_USERNAME: ${MQTT_USERNAME:-}
      MQTT_PASSWORD: ${MQTT_PASSWORD:-}
      LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL:-INFO}

  4. Below the editor, find Environment variables. Select Add an environment variable for each value in the table. You can also select Advanced mode and paste NAME=value lines.

    Variable Required Example Meaning SPA_IP Yes 192.168.1.100 Address of the RS485-to-TCP adapter (or the ProLink module) MQTT_BROKER Yes 192.168.1.7 Address of the MQTT broker MQTT_USERNAME If the broker needs a login spa Broker user name MQTT_PASSWORD If the broker needs a login Broker password SPA_PORT No 8899 TCP port of the adapter. 4257 for a ProLink module SPA_DEFINITION No jacuzzi_j235 Tub definition. jacuzzi_j345 for a J345 SPA_TRANSMIT No false Leave false until you have read Safety LOG_LEVEL No INFO DEBUG for more detail SPA2MQTT_TAG No 2 Image tag. See Releases and versions

    The stack refuses to deploy if SPA_IP or MQTT_BROKER is missing. This stops a container that would only log connection errors.

    For a Jacuzzi J345 with a ProLink module, the J345 guide lists the values.

  5. Select Deploy the stack.

In Home Assistant, open Settings > Devices & services > MQTT. A device named after the tub definition, for example Jacuzzi J235, appears within a few seconds. Its buttons and the setpoint show as unavailable while transmit is off. That is expected.

Home Assistant OS host addresses

If the MQTT broker is the Mosquitto add-on on the same Home Assistant OS host, set MQTT_BROKER to the host's LAN address. The name core-mosquitto resolves only on the add-on network, not on the network that Portainer stacks use.

docs.title: Update
docs.text:
The tag 2 follows every 2.x.y release. To get the newest image for the tag:

  1. Open Stacks > spa2mqtt.
  2. Select Editor, then Update the stack.
  3. Turn on Re-pull image and redeploy, then select Update.

Without the re-pull option, Portainer reuses the image that it already has. On some Portainer versions the same action is named Pull and redeploy.

docs.title: Roll back or pin a version
docs.text: Set SPA2MQTT_TAG to a full version, for example 2.0.0, then update the stack. The container stays on that version until you change the variable.

docs.title: B. Stack from the repository (build)
docs.text:
This method makes Portainer clone the repository and build the image on the Docker host. Building takes a few minutes and needs internet access to PyPI and Docker Hub.

  1. Select Stacks > Add stack, set Name to spa2mqtt, and select Repository.
  2. Set Repository URL to https://github.com/srleach/spa2mqtt.
  3. Set Repository reference to a release tag such as refs/tags/v2.0.0. A tag gives you a known version. refs/heads/main builds the newest code.
  4. Set Compose path to docker-compose.yml. This is the development compose file at the repository root. It builds from source and has no bind mounts.
  5. Add the same Environment variables as in method A. SPA2MQTT_TAG has no effect here.
  6. Select Deploy the stack.

To update, change the reference if needed, then select Pull and redeploy on the stack page. Portainer fetches the repository again and rebuilds the image.

docs.title: Set or change environment variables
docs.text: Open Stacks > spa2mqtt > Editor. The Environment variables section is below the compose editor. Change a value, then select Update the stack. Portainer recreates the container with the new values.

docs.title: Read the logs
docs.text:
1. Open Containers and select spa2mqtt.
  2. Select Logs.
  3. Turn on Auto-refresh logs to follow new lines.

The log shows the adapter and broker connections, warnings, and whether transmit is enabled.

docs.title: Run the read-only monitor
docs.text:
The monitor decodes the bus and never transmits. Stop the spa2mqtt container first, because most adapters accept only one TCP client.

  1. Open Containers, select spa2mqtt, and select Stop.
  2. Select Containers > Add container.
  3. Set Name to spa2mqtt-monitor and Image to ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt:2.
  4. Under Advanced container settings > Command & logging, set Command to spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.100 (your adapter's address). Add -p PORT and -d DEFINITION if yours are not 8899 and jacuzzi_j235, for example spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.50 -p 4257 -d jacuzzi_j345. Set Console to Interactive & TTY.
  5. Under Restart policy, select Never.
  6. Select Deploy the container, then open its Logs. A report appears at once and then every 10 seconds.
  7. When you are done, stop and remove spa2mqtt-monitor, then start spa2mqtt again.

If you have a shell on the Docker host, this one line does the same:

docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt:2 spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.100

docs.title: Enable transmit
docs.text: Read Safety first. Then set SPA_TRANSMIT to true in the stack's environment variables and update the stack. The log shows TRANSMIT ENABLED. To go back to receive-only, set it to false and update the stack again.

docs.title: Limits of an environment-only setup
docs.text: The ha: settings (unique_id_prefix, legacy_topics, device_name and others) and a USB serial adapter need a config.yml, and Portainer under Home Assistant OS cannot mount one. The defaults suit almost every install: the device name and identifier come from the tub definition. If you need to change them, run spa2mqtt with Docker Compose on a host that allows bind mounts.

docs.title: Jacuzzi J235 (EW11A or ESP32)
docs.text:
This guide sets up spa2mqtt for a Jacuzzi J235: a J-200 series tub from 2018 with the encrypted Balboa-family control board. spa2mqtt reads the board's RS485 bus through an RS485-to-TCP adapter such as the Elfin EW11A, or through an ESP32 running the ESPHome component. The definition ID is jacuzzi_j235. It is the default, so most settings on this page are the defaults.

Tested on the project's own tub

Every sensor was checked against labelled captures from the project's own J235. Transmit runs on that tub through the MQTT bridge and an EW11A (November 2026): the board granted the bridge channel 0x11, and the buttons, Temperature Set Control and the switches act at the topside. Start receive-only on a new install, and watch the topside for the first commands.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text: Each row has the evidence status from the definition. Confirmed means a labelled capture shows the change at the topside and the same change in the bytes. Hypothesis means a pattern in the data, or a name from another project, that no capture confirms. The wire protocol has the bytes.

docs.title: Read
docs.text: Entity Status Notes Current Water Temperature Confirmed °C, in 0.5 °C steps Target Water Temperature Confirmed °C, in 0.5 °C steps Pump 1 Speed Confirmed off, low or high Main Pump Status Confirmed Pump 1 on high: the jets Circulation Pump Status Confirmed Pump 1 running at any speed. The J235 has no separate circulation pump: it heats and filters on pump 1 low Secondary Pump Status Confirmed Pump 2. Single speed Heater Active Confirmed Light Mode Confirmed off, a colour name, blend or blend paused. MQTT bridge only Filter Change Days, Water Change Days, UV Lamp Days Confirmed The topside menu's FC, H2O and UV countdowns, in days. Diagnostics Manual Circulation Call Hypothesis Never seen set on this tub Set Mode Active, Display State, Secondary Value Raw Mixed Diagnostics, disabled by default

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
All controls are unavailable until you enable transmit.

Entity What it does Temperature Increment, Temperature Decrement One press of Temp up or Temp down. The first press only opens the set screen Temperature Set Control Presses Temp up or down until the setpoint matches. Range 20 to 40 °C, step 0.5 Pump 1 Button, Pump 2 Button, Light Button One press of that topside button. Pump 1 steps off, low, high, off Pump 1 (switch) The jets. Presses Pump 1 until pump 1 is on high, or off. MQTT bridge only Pump 1 Low (switch) Pump 1 low speed. Its "off" is pump 1 fully off, so from low it steps through high to off. MQTT bridge only Pump 2 (switch) Presses Pump 2 when it is not already in the state you chose. MQTT bridge only Light (switch) Presses Light until the light is on or off, about 7.5 s between presses. MQTT bridge only

The button codes (0x01, 0x02, 0x04, 0x05, 0x12) were confirmed from the topside's own presses in a capture. The bridge sends the same codes.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Light colour, brightness and blend as direct controls. The light has one button: see Known limits.
  • Clock setting, filter cycles, heat mode, ClearRay and the menu. The maintenance countdowns are read only: reset them at the topside.
  • Fahrenheit. The board gives no unit flag, and every capture is in °C. The definition is Celsius only.

docs.title: Hardware path
docs.text:
The bridge and the ESP32 both connect to the RS485 header on the control board. The header is meant for a second topside panel and is usually free. It carries 12 V, 0 V, A and B. Isolate the spa at its breaker before you open the equipment bay. Read Safety first.

Item Value Bus RS485, 115200 baud, 8N1 EW11A mode TCP server, port 8899, transparent ESP32 Any ESP32 with a 3.3 V RS485 transceiver. See Hardware and wiring Bus address the bridge sends from A channel the board gives it on the first command. Set at run time, not by the definition

Connect A to A and B to B. If no status frames arrive and the serial settings are right, swap A and B: a swap does no damage. Power the adapter or the ESP32 from its own supply unless you know the rating of the header's 12 V.

The EW11A accepts one TCP client at a time. Stop the v1 bridge, a monitor or any other tool before you start spa2mqtt. The v1 bridge must be stopped in any case: it claims a bus channel at start-up.

docs.title: Install with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Follow Install with Docker Compose. The defaults in .env.example are for this tub. Set the addresses:

SPA_IP=192.168.1.100
SPA_PORT=8899
SPA_DEFINITION=jacuzzi_j235
SPA_TRANSMIT=false
MQTT_BROKER=192.168.1.7
MQTT_PORT=1883
MQTT_USERNAME=
MQTT_PASSWORD=

docs.title: Install with Portainer on Home Assistant OS
docs.text:
Follow Install with Portainer, method A, with the stack file deploy/portainer-stack.yml and these variables:

Variable Value SPA_IP EW11A address, for example 192.168.1.100 SPA_PORT 8899, the default SPA_DEFINITION jacuzzi_j235, the default SPA_TRANSMIT false MQTT_BROKER Broker address. For the Mosquitto add-on, use the Home Assistant host's LAN address: core-mosquitto does not resolve from a Portainer stack MQTT_PORT 1883 MQTT_USERNAME, MQTT_PASSWORD Broker login, if the broker needs one LOG_LEVEL INFO

SPA_IP and MQTT_BROKER are required, and the stack refuses to deploy without them.

docs.title: Install with ESPHome
docs.text:
Follow ESPHome: Hardware and wiring, then Build and flash. The package esphome/packages/jacuzzi_j235.yaml lists every J235 entity the component supports.

The component decodes the status frame only. It has no Light Mode sensor and none of the switches. The buttons and Temperature Set Control are the same.

docs.title: Upgrade from the v1 bridge
docs.text:
Version 2 replaces the v1 bridge in place. It keeps the device (185569045), the unique_ids and the discovery topics, so every entity keeps its ID and history. Your v1 config.yml and VARIANT_DEFINITION still work. Two changes matter:

  • Buttons and Temperature Set Control are unavailable until you enable transmit. v1 transmitted by default.
  • Main Pump Status is pump 1 on high. Circulation Pump Status is pump 1 at any speed.

See Upgrade from v1 for the full list.

docs.title: Verify, receive-only first
docs.text:
With transmit off, the bridge and the ESP32 never write to the bus.

  1. Run the read-only monitor once (Getting started). The checksum error count stays at or near zero. A high count means a wrong baud rate or swapped A and B.
  2. In Home Assistant, open Settings > Devices & services. A device named Jacuzzi J235 appears under MQTT, or under ESPHome for the component. The controls show as unavailable. That is expected.

  3. Compare with the topside:

    Check How Current Water Temperature Same number as the topside display Target Water Temperature Press Temp up twice at the topside: the first press opens the set screen, the second adds 0.5 °C. Then step back Pump 1 Speed Press the pump 1 button three times: low, high, off Pump 2 Press the pump 2 button on and off Heater Active Raise the setpoint above the water temperature. Pump 1 starts on low, then the heater follows about a minute later Light Mode Press the light button. MQTT bridge only Filter Change Days, Water Change Days, UV Lamp Days The FC, H2O and UV values in the topside menu

docs.title: Enable transmit
docs.text:
Read Safety first.

First commands on your tub

The channel claim works on the project's J235 with the MQTT bridge. Your board, adapter or ESP32 wiring may differ. Have someone at the topside for the first commands.

What the bridge or the ESP32 sends:

  1. At start-up, nothing.
  2. On the first command, a channel request. The J235's only polled channel (0x10) is the topside panel, and it answers every poll, so there is no free channel to reuse. spa2mqtt asks the board for a new one when the board offers it, about once a second, and acknowledges the answer.
  3. Then one button press each time the board polls that channel. When nothing is queued, it stays silent.
  4. If another device answers on the same channel, spa2mqtt goes back to listening.

For the MQTT bridge, set SPA_TRANSMIT=true and recreate the container or update the stack. The log shows TRANSMIT ENABLED. For ESPHome, set transmit: true in the spa_bus: block and install the firmware: the Bus State sensor shows claiming, requested, then ready (0x..) on the first command.

Test in this order, one command at a time, and watch the topside after each:

  1. Pump 2 Button, twice: on, then off.
  2. Light Button, then wait ten seconds and press it again to turn the light off.
  3. Pump 1 Button, three times: low, high, off.
  4. Temperature Increment, twice, then Temperature Decrement once. The setpoint rises 0.5 °C and falls back.
  5. Temperature Set Control, 0.5 °C up, then back.
  6. The switches, last.

To stop, set transmit off again. If the topside shows an error, isolate the spa at the breaker and wait before you switch it on again.

docs.title: Send captures back
docs.text:
A capture of something new on this tub helps, in particular a session with commands and the menu. spa2mqtt capture is read-only and keeps only the frames that changed:

docker run --rm -it ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt:2 spa2mqtt capture 192.168.1.100 -o j235.log

For a session with labels, use tools/capture.py. Stop the bridge first: the EW11A accepts one client. See Monitor and capture for both, and Contribute a capture to share the file.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Celsius only. The board's status gives no unit flag. Keep the topside in °C.
  • The first temperature press only opens the set screen. Temperature Increment and Temperature Decrement behave like the topside. Temperature Set Control accounts for it.
  • Pump 1 Low may not turn off. The board runs pump 1 low by itself to heat or filter. While it does, pressing pump 1 cannot reach off, and the switch gives up after a fixed number of presses.
  • The light has one button. A press within a few seconds of the last one steps the colour. A press after a pause turns the light off. The Light switch waits about 7.5 s between presses for that reason. There is no direct colour or brightness command.
  • ESPHome has no lights frame. Light Mode and the switches are MQTT bridge only.

Open questions that a capture or a test at the tub would answer:

  1. Where are the filter cycle settings and the heat mode? A capture while they are changed at the topside would settle it.
  2. What does Manual Circulation Call show, if anything?
  3. What are the button codes for ClearRay and the menu on this tub?

The wire protocol lists the unknown bytes.

docs.title: Jacuzzi J345 (ProLink)
docs.text:
This guide sets up the MQTT bridge for a Jacuzzi J345: a J-300 series tub with an unencrypted control board, reached through the original Jacuzzi ProLink Wi-Fi module. Older threads and file names call this tub a "J335". The definition ID is jacuzzi_j345.

Nobody on the project has this tub

The definition was decoded from five logs that the tub's owner shared, and checked against pyjacuzzi. The project has not run it against the tub. Start receive-only, compare every value with the topside, and report what you see.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text: Each row has the evidence status from the definition. Confirmed means a capture shows a command and the tub's reaction, or the same change from the topside in several captures. Inferred means the captures agree with pyjacuzzi but nobody compared the value with the tub. Hypothesis means a pattern in the data only. The plain protocol reference has the bytes.

docs.title: Read
docs.text: Entity Status Notes Current Water Temperature Inferred Whole °F. Never compared with the topside display Target Water Temperature Confirmed Whole °F Pump 1, Pump 2 Confirmed On or off. A low speed, if a pump has one, would read as off Circulation Pump Inferred Heater Active Hypothesis Follows the thermostat in the captures. No reference names the bit Light Mode Confirmed off, a colour name, blend or blend paused Light Brightness Confirmed Percent Secondary Temperature, Flow Switch, CLEARRAY Days Remaining Inferred Diagnostics Set Mode Active, Reminder Active, Celsius Mode, Display State, State Raw, Error Code, Light Red, Light Green, Light Blue Mixed Diagnostics, disabled by default

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
All controls are unavailable until you enable transmit.

Entity Status What it sends Temperature Set Control Confirmed for 90, 100 and 101 °F One set-temperature frame. Range 80 to 104 °F, step 1 Pump 1 Button, Pump 2 Button Confirmed One button frame. Each press toggles the pump Pump 1, Pump 2 (switches) Confirmed The same button frame, sent only when the pump is not already in the state you chose. One frame, no retry Light White … Light Aqua (nine buttons) Confirmed One light frame that selects the colour Light Brightness Confirmed for 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, with a colour already on One light frame. 0 turns the lights off. Select a colour first: see Known limits

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• The ESPHome component. This tub is bridge-only.
  • Temperature up and down buttons, the topside light and colour buttons, UV and the menu. Their codes come from a different tub.
  • Clock setting, locks, filter cycles and heat mode.
  • Pump 3 and the blower.
  • Light blend mode as a control. pyjacuzzi notes that the board refuses it as a direct command. Raising the brightness from 0 may start it: see Known limits.
  • Celsius. The definition is Fahrenheit only, and the bridge refuses to send a setpoint while the tub reports Celsius mode.

docs.title: Hardware path
docs.text:
There is nothing to wire. The bridge connects to the ProLink module over your network.

Item Value Address The ProLink module's LAN address. Find it in your router's client list and give it a fixed lease TCP port 4257 Adapter None. Do not use the EW11A settings (port 8899) Bus address the bridge sends from 0x0A, the ProLink's own address. Set by the definition

The ProLink is assumed to serve one client at a time. Stop pyjacuzzi, the v1 bridge and any other tool before you start spa2mqtt. Whether the official app can run at the same time is unknown.

docs.title: Install with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Follow Install with Docker Compose with these values in .env:

SPA_IP=192.168.1.50
SPA_PORT=4257
SPA_DEFINITION=jacuzzi_j345
SPA_TRANSMIT=false
MQTT_BROKER=192.168.1.7
MQTT_PORT=1883
MQTT_USERNAME=
MQTT_PASSWORD=

docs.title: Install with Portainer on Home Assistant OS
docs.text:
Portainer under Home Assistant OS cannot mount files, so every setting is an environment variable. Follow Install with Portainer, method A. Use the same stack file, deploy/portainer-stack.yml, and set these variables:

Variable Value SPA_IP ProLink address, for example 192.168.1.50 SPA_PORT 4257 SPA_DEFINITION jacuzzi_j345 SPA_TRANSMIT false MQTT_BROKER Broker address. For the Mosquitto add-on, use the Home Assistant host's LAN address: core-mosquitto does not resolve from a Portainer stack MQTT_PORT 1883 MQTT_USERNAME, MQTT_PASSWORD Broker login, if the broker needs one LOG_LEVEL INFO

SPA_PORT and SPA_DEFINITION matter most: the defaults are for the J235 behind an EW11A. SPA_IP and MQTT_BROKER are required, and the stack refuses to deploy without them.

Coming from the v1 debug image

The old name jacuzzi_j335_unencrypted_farenheit still selects this definition, and VARIANT_DEFINITION is still read. The stack file passes only the variables in the table, so set SPA_DEFINITION there.

The image must include this definition. If the log says unknown tub definition 'jacuzzi_j345', the image is older than this guide: update it (Update).

docs.title: Verify, receive-only first
docs.text:
With SPA_TRANSMIT=false the bridge cannot change the tub. Nothing is written to the ProLink.

  1. In Home Assistant, open Settings > Devices & services > MQTT. A device named Jacuzzi J345 appears within a few seconds. The controls show as unavailable. That is expected.

  2. Stand at the tub, or ask someone to, and compare with the topside:

    Check How Current Water Temperature Same number as the topside display Target Water Temperature Change the setpoint at the topside by 1 °F and back Pump 1, Pump 2 Press each jets button on and off Circulation Pump Is the circulation pump running? Heater Active Does it match the heater indicator on the topside? Light Brightness Switch the light on at the topside and step its brightness

  3. Report what matched and what did not in discussion 13. A value that matches moves from inferred to confirmed. A value that does not match is just as useful.

The log names the fields that are still hypotheses at start-up. Any time the bridge decodes is the tub's own clock. In the captures that clock runs about 51 minutes slow.

docs.title: Enable transmit
docs.text:
Read Safety first.

First commands on a tub the project has never driven

The frames the bridge sends are the frames pyjacuzzi sent to this tub in a captured session, byte for byte, and the test suite checks that. That shows the bytes are right. It does not show that the bridge's timing suits the ProLink. Have someone at the tub for the first commands.

What the bridge sends:

  1. At start-up, nothing.
  2. On the first command after each connection, one connection check frame (7e 07 0a bf 19 01 00 95 7e). pyjacuzzi sends this first, and the tub answers it. Whether commands need it is unknown.
  3. Then one frame per command, at least four status frames (about 1.2 seconds) apart. There is no retry. The next status frame shows whether the tub obeyed.

Set SPA_TRANSMIT=true and update the stack. The log shows TRANSMIT ENABLED. Then test in this order, one command at a time, and watch the topside after each:

  1. A light colour, for example Light Blue. Then Light Brightness to 0 to turn the lights off.
  2. Pump 2 Button, twice: on, then off.
  3. Pump 1 Button, twice.
  4. Temperature Set Control, 1 °F up, then back.

Turn the lights off with brightness 0

A colour button writes all four light records in the tub. The topside changes only the first one. Set Light Brightness to 0 to clear all four.

To stop, set SPA_TRANSMIT=false and update the stack. If the topside shows an error, isolate the spa at the breaker and wait before you switch it on again.

docs.title: Send captures back
docs.text:
A capture with the times of your actions settles the open questions below. The monitor is read-only and can print the capture into the container log, so it works without a mounted file.

  1. Stop the spa2mqtt container.
  2. In Portainer, select Containers > Add container. Set Name to spa2mqtt-monitor and Image to ghcr.io/srleach/spa2mqtt:2.

  3. Under Advanced container settings > Command & logging, set Command to:

    spa2mqtt monitor 192.168.1.50 -p 4257 -d jacuzzi_j345 --record -

    Set Console to Interactive & TTY. Under Restart policy, select Never.

  4. Deploy the container and open its Logs. Turn Display timestamps off. Raise Lines from the default 100 to 5000 or more: the capture adds about four lines per second.

  5. Do one thing at a time at the topside, about ten seconds apart, and write down the time of each: the displayed water temperature, each pump on and off, the light, the setpoint up and down.
  6. Copy the whole log and post it in discussion 13 with your notes. The log shows the ProLink's LAN address in the line that starts spa2mqtt monitor: and in every line that contains connected to. Remove the address from those lines, or delete them, before you post. Only the RX lines are needed.
  7. Stop and remove spa2mqtt-monitor, then start spa2mqtt again.

The lines that matter look like 1748000000.123 RX 7e25ffaf16…. The report lines between them are ignored when the log is replayed.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• Fahrenheit only. Celsius mode on this board was never captured. Keep the topside in °F. If the Celsius Mode bit is set, the bridge refuses Temperature Set Control and logs a warning: pyjacuzzi sends half degrees Celsius in the same byte in that mode, so "80" would ask for 40 °C. The bridge also refuses the setpoint until it has decoded one status frame. The temperature readings would still be published with the °F unit and would be wrong.
  • The setpoint range is 80 to 104 °F. These are the lowest and highest setpoints in any capture. Only 90, 100 and 101 were sent remotely. The bridge ignores a value outside the range and logs a warning. It does not clamp it.
  • Select a colour before you raise Light Brightness. In the capture, every non-zero brightness command was sent while a colour was on. pyjacuzzi's source says that raising the brightness from 0 is how the lights enter blend mode (src/jacuzziui.py L487–499). So a non-zero brightness sent while the lights are off is expected to start the colour cycle, not a steady light. Nobody has seen this on this tub.
  • Light Brightness steps by 20. Those are the values the capture shows accepted. The topside's own steps (100, 66, 33) still display correctly.

Open questions that a capture or a test at the tub would answer:

  1. Is the connection check needed before commands work?
  2. Does the ProLink accept a second TCP client, or the official app at the same time?
  3. Does the water temperature match the topside? What does the second sensor measure?
  4. Is Heater Active the heater? It rests on one bit that no reference names.
  5. Does either pump have a low speed? Is there a pump 3, a blower or a UV button?
  6. What does the tub do with a setpoint outside 80 to 104 °F? The bridge never sends one.
  7. Does a non-zero brightness sent while the lights are off start blend mode, as pyjacuzzi's source says?
  8. Why did the CLEARRAY counter fall from 364 to 0 in six days?

The plain protocol reference lists the unknown bytes.
